Play it again and tap the beat with your finger. Notice which notes hold for more than one tap.

method_card.title: Following a score while it plays
method_card.content:
In the exam the music is playing while you look at the notation. You are never asked to read it in silence. So the first skill is simply keeping your place: knowing which mark on the page is making the sound you are hearing right now.

Press play on each example below and watch. Do not try to name anything yet.

Once you can follow a line, everything else in this unit is just labelling what you are already tracking.

exam_context.title: Why this comes first
exam_context.content: Section A plays music and may show you up to 12 bars of it. Every question about that notation assumes you can keep your place while it sounds. Get that, and naming time signatures and note values is straightforward.

options: The hollow note was played by a different instrument
gold.question: Play Extract A again. Its last note is hollow and the others are filled in. What did you hear that matches?
gold.explanation: A hollow head means a longer note, and you heard it hold while the filled ones went past in a beat each. You have just read a note value off the page by ear.

gold.question: Play Extract F. The performance departs from the printed score in exactly one place. In which bar?
gold.explanation: Bar 3 is printed C–E–G–C, climbing evenly. What sounds on the third beat is a note higher than the printed G, so the line jumps further than the page says. Following the printed notes while listening is exactly what Section A asks of you when it prints an extract of the music being played.

options: Bar 1 — a note is played too short
Bar 2 — a note is held too long and the next one is missed
Bar 3 — the last note is too low
Bar 2 — two notes are swapped in order
gold.question: Play Extract G. Again the performance departs from the score once. What is wrong, and where?
gold.explanation: The score prints four separate notes climbing through bar 2. In the performance the first of them is held for two beats, so the note that should follow it never sounds — the bar still lasts four beats, which is why it is easy to miss. Checking rhythm against the page, not just pitch, is the harder half of the skill.

gold.question: Play Extract H. One printed note is not the pitch you hear. Which bar?
gold.explanation: Bar 3 is printed as the same rising figure as bar 1 — C, D, E, F. The fourth beat sounds well above the printed F, so the line jumps instead of stepping. Bars 1 and 2 are exactly as written, which is what makes the repeat worth checking.

gold.question: Play Extract I. Every pitch is correct, but one note is not the printed length. Where?
gold.explanation: Bar 2 is printed as four even crotchets. The second one is held for two beats, so the third printed note never sounds and the bar still totals four. On a single repeated pitch there is no melodic clue at all — only the rhythm gives it away.

gold.question: Play Extract J. Something printed is skipped. What, and where?
gold.explanation: The score climbs one step per note throughout. In bar 2 the performance goes F then A, missing the printed G, so the bar contains two notes where three are written and the climb jumps. Counting notes per bar against the page catches this faster than listening for a wrong pitch.

bronze.question: Play Extract A. How many notes are there?
bronze.explanation: Five notes light up: four short ones, then a long one to finish. Counting the highlights is the most reliable way to check you are following the right line.

options: It stays on the same note
bronze.question: Play Extract C. Does the tune rise or fall?
bronze.explanation: Each note sits lower on the stave than the one before, and the sound drops with it. Higher on the page always means higher in pitch.

bronze.question: Play Extract B. Which note is held longest?
bronze.explanation: The final note keeps the highlight for four beats — a whole bar. The second note holds for two, and the first and third for one each.

options: Neither — it is one long note
bronze.question: Play Extract K. Which bar contains more notes?
bronze.explanation: Bar 2 lights up four times, bar 1 only twice. Both bars last the same length of time, so the notes in bar 2 must each be shorter — which is what the hollow and filled heads are telling you on the page.

silver.question: Play Extract D. In which bar does the tune stop climbing and hold?
silver.explanation: Bar 1 climbs a note at a time. In bar 2 the highlight stays on the same pitch for two longer notes before moving up once more in bar 3. Bar lines are the thin vertical strokes crossing the stave.

silver.question: Play Extract E. Which describes its shape best?
silver.explanation: The line climbs for three notes, then comes back down to where it started. You can see the arch on the page and hear it at the same time — that matching is the whole skill.

options: It rises, then falls back to where it began
silver.question: Play Extract L. What shape does the melody make?
silver.explanation: The line climbs for four notes and then comes back down to its starting pitch. Seeing the arch on the page and hearing it at the same time is the whole point of following a score.

options: The notes are played very quietly
The notes are played by a different instrument
silver.question: Play Extract M. What happens on beats 2 and 4 of the first bar?
silver.explanation: The highlight goes out because nothing is sounding. Those gaps are rests, and they are written on the stave just as deliberately as the notes.

steps.label: Step 1 — count the highlights
steps.content: Play it and count how many times a note lights up. Four.

steps.label: Step 2 — watch how long each stays lit
steps.content: The second note stays lit for two taps of the beat while the first and third get one each. The last one holds longest of all.

steps.label: Step 3 — check it against the page
steps.content: The notes that held longer are the hollow ones. Filled notes went past quickly. That is the clue you will use for the rest of the unit.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Four notes. The last is longest, and the second is longer than the first and third.

steps: Find the time signature. The top number is how many beats fill a bar.
Is the top number 2, 3 or 4 (simple) or 6, 9 or 12 (compound)?
For each note, check the head first, then count the tails.
Look for dots. A dot adds half of that note's own value.
method_card.title: Reading how long a note lasts
method_card.content:
In Lesson 1 you followed a line while it played. Now put names to the lengths you were already hearing.

Then the metre: how the beats themselves are grouped and divided.

options: Bar 1 — the notes are played too fast
Bar 2 — the first note is lengthened and the second shortened
Bar 3 — the last note is too short
Bar 2 — a note is missing altogether
gold.question: Play Extract D. The pitches are all correct, but one bar is not played as printed. Which one, and what changed?
gold.explanation: Bar 2 is printed as four even crotchets. What sounds is a long-short pair followed by two even notes — the first note borrows half a beat from the second, giving the dotted, lopsided feel. The bar still totals four beats, which is exactly why this is easy to miss unless you are reading along.

options: They cannot — six quavers always sound the same
3/4 groups them as three pairs, 6/8 as two threes
3/4 is simple because it uses crotchets and 6/8 is compound because it uses quavers
gold.question: Why can a piece in 3/4 and a piece in 6/8 both have six quavers in a bar, yet feel completely different?
gold.explanation: Same six quavers, different grouping. 3/4 is three crotchet beats each splitting in two; 6/8 is two dotted-crotchet beats each splitting in three. The beaming on the page shows you which, and the accent pattern lets you hear it.

gold.question: Play Extract E. One bar is not played with the printed rhythm. Which?
gold.explanation: Bar 2 is printed as four crotchets. What sounds is crotchet, minim, crotchet — the second note takes the third note's beat. The bar still lasts four beats, so only reading along reveals it.

gold.question: Play Extract F. One bar is not played in even threes. Which?
gold.explanation: 6/8 gives two beats, each splitting into three EVEN quavers. Bar 2 is played long-short, long-short — a lopsided swing the page does not ask for. The beaming still shows even groups of three, so the performance and the notation disagree.

gold.question: Play Extract G. One dotted note is not held for its printed length. Which bar?
gold.explanation: Every bar is printed as a dotted minim (3 beats) plus a crotchet. In bar 2 the first note is held for only two beats and the second stretches to two, so the dotted long-short shape becomes two equal halves and the dot is effectively ignored.

bronze.question: A note has a hollow head and a stem, and no tail. How long is it?
bronze.explanation: That is a minim: 2 beats. Hollow means long, and the stem — the plain vertical line — never changes the length. Only a semibreve, which has no stem at all, is longer.

bronze.question: Play Extract B. How many beats does the first note last?
bronze.explanation: A hollow head with a dot: the minim is 2 beats and the dot adds half of 2, making 3. Tap the beat while it plays and you will feel it hold for three.

bronze.question: A piece has a 6/8 time signature. Is it simple or compound time?
bronze.explanation: The TOP number decides it: 6, 9 or 12 means compound, so each beat divides into three. The bottom number only tells you which note gets the beat.

bronze.question: Play Extract H. Which note lasts longest, and how many beats?
bronze.explanation: The last note is hollow with a stem — a minim, 2 beats — while the first two are filled crotchets of 1 beat each. Together they fill the four-beat bar.

silver.question: Play Extract A. How many beats are in each bar?
silver.explanation: The time signature reads 3 over 4 — three crotchet beats per bar. Count the highlight: it moves three times before the bar line each time.

options: Into two, so it is simple time
Into three, so it is compound time
Into four, so it is simple time
silver.question: Play Extract C. How do the beats divide?
silver.explanation: You can hear the quavers grouping in threes, and see them beamed in threes on the page. 6/8 is compound duple: two beats a bar, each a dotted crotchet worth three quavers.

silver.question: A dotted crotchet lasts how long?
silver.explanation: A crotchet is 1 beat and the dot adds half of 1. The rule is always 'half of the note's own value' — which is why the same dot makes a minim 3 but a crotchet 1½.

options: Four — there are four notes in bar 2
Three — the time signature reads 3 over 4, and each bar totals three beats
Two — the first bar has two notes
silver.question: Play Extract I. How many beats are in each bar, and how do you know?
silver.explanation: The top number of the time signature gives the beats per bar. Bar 1 is a minim plus a crotchet (2 + 1) and bar 2 is three crotchets — both total three.

steps.label: Step 1 — read the head
steps.content: It is hollow, so it is at least a minim: 2 beats.

steps.label: Step 2 — check for a dot
steps.content: There is a dot after it. A dot adds half the note's own value, and half of 2 is 1.

steps.label: Step 3 — confirm by ear
steps.content: Play it and tap the beat. The first note holds for three taps before the next one arrives.

steps: Play it once and just watch whether the line rises, falls, or arches.
Ask whether it moves to the next line or space (step) or jumps (leap).
Look between the clef and the time signature for the key signature.
Watch for sharps, flats or naturals written in front of individual notes.
method_card.title: Reading pitch and shape
method_card.content:
Higher on the page is higher in sound. Everything in this lesson follows from that.

Then two things that tell you which notes the piece is using at all.

gold.question: Play Extract D. The rhythm is correct throughout, but one printed note is not the pitch you hear. Where?
gold.explanation: The score prints bar 2 as a continuing stepwise climb: G, A, B, C. What sounds on the second beat is well above the printed A — the line jumps up and then has to come back down to B, breaking the smooth ascent you can see on the page.

options: Shape is a musical feature you can point to in the score and hear at the same time
gold.question: Why is describing the shape of a melody more useful in the exam than saying it 'sounds nice'?
gold.explanation: Section A rewards naming a feature and saying where it happens. 'The melody rises stepwise to a peak in bar 3, then falls by leap' is evidence; 'it sounds nice' is not.

gold.question: Play Extract E. The arch shape is printed twice. One note differs the second time. Which beat?
gold.explanation: Bars 1 and 3 are printed identically — C, E, G, C. On the fourth beat of bar 3 you hear a note below the printed top C, so the second arch does not reach as high as the first. Comparing a repeat against its first appearance is a standard Section A task.

gold.question: Play Extract F. The line is printed entirely stepwise, but the performance leaps once. Where?
gold.explanation: The printed line walks up and back down by step throughout. On the last beat of bar 2 the performance jumps past the printed C, breaking the conjunct movement you can see on the page.

gold.question: Play Extract G. The key signature shows two sharps. Which note is played as if it were not sharpened?
gold.explanation: The key signature sharpens every F and C in the piece, so the third note is printed as F sharp. It sounds a semitone lower — an F natural — which is why the line loses its brightness at that point. A key signature applies all the way through, not just to bar 1.

bronze.question: Play Extract A. How does the melody move?
bronze.explanation: Every note moves to the next line or space, up then back down. Smooth, joined movement like this is called conjunct.

bronze.question: Play Extract B. How does this melody move?
bronze.explanation: The notes jump across several lines at a time, and it sounds angular. Movement by leap is called disjunct.

options: At the end of the first bar
Between the clef and the time signature
Next to every note it affects
bronze.question: Where in a score do you find the key signature?
bronze.explanation: It sits immediately after the clef, before the time signature, and it applies for the whole piece — not just the first bar.

bronze.question: Play Extract H. How does the melody move overall?
bronze.explanation: Each pair of notes sits higher on the stave than the pair before, and the sound climbs with them. Higher on the page always means higher in pitch.

silver.question: Play Extract C. Which best describes its shape?
silver.explanation: Bar 1 descends step by step; bar 2 climbs back up. Being able to describe the contour of a line — rising, falling, arching, or a wave — earns marks in Section A.

options: To that note and any repeat of it for the rest of that bar
To the rest of the piece
silver.question: A sharp is written in front of one note in the middle of a bar. How far does it apply?
silver.explanation: An accidental holds for the remainder of the bar it appears in, then lapses at the next bar line. That is what distinguishes it from a key signature.

silver.question: Which word describes a melody that moves mainly by step?
silver.explanation: Conjunct means stepwise; disjunct means leaping. Using the right term rather than 'it goes up smoothly' is what turns a description into a mark.

options: Neither — it stays on one note
Conjunct — it uses only four notes
silver.question: Play Extract I. Is this movement conjunct or disjunct?
silver.explanation: The notes jump across several lines and spaces rather than moving to the neighbouring one, and it sounds angular. Movement by leap is disjunct; stepwise movement is conjunct.

steps.label: Step 1 — look before you listen
steps.content: The notes are not on neighbouring lines and spaces; there are gaps between them.

steps.label: Step 2 — play it
steps.content: It sounds bold and jumpy rather than smooth. Each move covers noticeable distance.

steps.label: Step 3 — name it
steps.content: Movement by leap is disjunct. Movement by step is conjunct. Section A uses both words.

steps: Scan below the stave for letters — those are dynamics.
Look above and below the note heads for dots (staccato) and curved lines (slurs).
Check the clef at the start of each stave before you read any pitch.
In a full score, read top to bottom: woodwind, brass, percussion, strings.
method_card.title: Reading expression and forces

gold.question: Play Extract F. The articulation is played correctly, but one printed note is not the pitch you hear. Where?
gold.explanation: Bar 2 is printed as a stepwise climb G, A, B, C. On the third beat you hear the top C arrive a beat early, so the printed B never sounds and the note repeats instead. The staccato bar before it is played exactly as written, which is what makes this one harder to locate.

options: It starts quietly and gets louder, and sounds quite smooth
It begins p and changes to f at bar 3; the notes are unmarked, so they are played normally rather than staccato or slurred
gold.question: A Section A question shows you this extract and asks you to 'describe the dynamics and articulation'. Which answer would score best?
gold.explanation: The strongest answer names the marking, translates it, and says WHERE it happens. A bare list of terms shows recognition but not reading; a vague impression shows neither.

gold.question: Play Extract G. One printed articulation is not what you hear. Which bar?
gold.explanation: Bar 3 is printed with staccato dots but is played smoothly and joined, with no gaps between the notes. Bars 1 and 2 are played exactly as marked, so the contrast you can hear between them is correct and only the third bar disagrees with the page.

gold.question: Play Extract H. The dynamics are played correctly. One pitch is not. Where?
gold.explanation: Bar 2 is printed as a stepwise climb G, A, B, C. The last beat sounds above the printed C, so the loud bar overshoots. The dynamic change at bar 2 is played exactly as written, which draws the ear away from the wrong note.

gold.question: Play Extract I. The articulation is right throughout, but one note is not the printed length. Where?
gold.explanation: The last bar is printed as a semibreve — four beats. It sounds for two and then stops, so the extract ends early. Checking that a final long note actually lasts its full value is easy to forget once the interesting material has gone past.

bronze.question: What does the marking mf mean?
bronze.explanation: mf is mezzo-forte: moderately loud. The ladder runs pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff — 'mezzo' means moderately, and it softens whichever word follows it.

options: Hold it for half as long again
bronze.question: A dot is printed above a note head. What does it tell the player?
bronze.explanation: A dot above or below the head means staccato: short and detached. Do not confuse it with a dot AFTER the head, which lengthens the note by half its value.

bronze.question: Play the longer extract. What dynamic does it begin with?
bronze.explanation: There is a p below the stave at the start, so it begins quiet. The f at bar 3 marks where it changes.

options: p then f — quiet, then loud
f then p — loud, then quiet
bronze.question: Look at Extract J. Which two dynamic markings appear, and in which order?
bronze.explanation: The f sits below the first note and the p below the last bar. A dynamic mark applies from where it appears until the next one changes it, so this extract begins loud and drops to quiet.

silver.question: In the longer extract, where does the dynamic change and what to?
silver.explanation: The f appears at the start of bar 3 and applies from there onward. A dynamic mark holds until the next one, so bars 1-2 are quiet and bars 3-5 loud.

options: The curve means play them smoothly joined; the dot means play that note short
The curve means repeat; the dot means louder
The curve means slow down; the dot means speed up
silver.question: What is the difference between a curved line over several different notes and a dot above one note?
silver.explanation: A slur asks for legato — smooth and connected. A staccato dot asks for the opposite: short, with a gap after it. They are often contrasted deliberately within one phrase.

options: The lines represent lower pitches, so a lower instrument or the left hand
The music has no key signature
silver.question: A stave begins with a bass clef. What does that tell you?
silver.explanation: The clef redefines what the five lines mean. Bass clef indicates lower-sounding parts — cello, bassoon, or a pianist's left hand. Always read the clef before any pitch.

options: Bar 1 is short and detached (staccato); bar 2 is smooth and joined (legato)
silver.question: Play Extract K. How does bar 2 differ from bar 1 in the way the notes are played?
silver.explanation: The dots above bar 1 mean staccato, so each note stops early and leaves a gap. The curved line over bar 2 is a slur, asking for legato — the notes run into one another.

steps.label: Step 1 — find the letters
steps.content: There is a p at the very start and an f at the beginning of bar 3.

steps.label: Step 2 — translate them
steps.content: p is piano, quiet. f is forte, loud.

steps.label: Step 3 — say where
steps.content: A mark applies from where it appears until the next one. So bars 1-2 are quiet and bars 3-5 are loud.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: It begins quietly (p) and becomes loud (f) at bar 3. Naming the marking AND the bar is what earns the mark.
